**Training buys reusable ability; inference buys effort on this particular problem.** Pretraining is like studying before an exam. Test-time compute is the time spent trying approaches, checking arithmetic, and revising during the exam. More study and more working time address different limitations. Chinchilla-style scaling asks how to divide a training budget between model size and data. Test-time scaling asks how to spend a request's budget after training. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556)

**Why extra attempts can help.** Suppose a model independently solves a problem with probability 0.2. Five attempts contain at least one correct solution with probability $1-(1-0.2)^5=0.67232$. That is a large improvement in candidate availability without changing model weights. But returning the correct candidate requires a verifier: five plausible answers plus a bad selector are not a 67% accurate system. Real attempts are also correlated, making this calculation an illustration rather than a forecast.

Additional compute can produce longer individual attempts, multiple independent solutions, or a search tree whose promising branches receive more effort. Use executable tests for code and reliable checks for mathematics when available. A model that cannot propose any useful intermediate step may gain little from more attempts.

**The economic comparison depends on traffic.** A training improvement is paid once and reused; extra reasoning is paid on every request. Compare total lifecycle compute and acceptable latency, not just parameter count. There is no theorem that extra reasoning always beats doubling parameters, and easy requests may need no extra search.

**Technical details and references.**

Pretraining scaling allocates a one-time compute budget between parameters and training tokens. Test-time scaling allocates per-request compute to additional samples, search, verification, or longer generated reasoning. The two are complementary, not replacements. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556)

$$C_{total}=C_{train}+Q\,C_{request}.$$

For a hard but solvable prompt, a capable smaller model plus a reliable verifier can use extra attempts more effectively than a modest parameter increase. For problems beyond the model's proposal capability or a weak verifier, extra inference may just repeat errors. Compare matched total FLOPs, latency, query volume, and difficulty. The “often beats doubling” claim is conditional on benchmark and budget; at very large serving volume, repeated inference costs can outweigh one-time training savings.
